question: What Is the Difference Between a Fractional CRO and a Fractional VP of Sales?
body:
## Direct Answer A fractional CRO owns the entire revenue engine — sales, marketing, customer success, RevOps, and pricing — as a part-time member of the executive team, while a fractional VP of Sales owns only the sales function: the team, the pipeline, and the quota. The CRO is a strategy-and-architecture hire who sets where revenue comes from across the whole funnel; the VP of Sales is an execution hire who makes a defined number happen inside one channel. Choosing wrong is expensive: a VP of Sales cannot fix a broken go-to-market motion, and a CRO is overqualified (and overpriced) for a company that just needs reps managed. The confusion is understandable because both are senior, both are "fractional" (part-time, embedded, typically 1–3 days a week), and both touch revenue. But they sit at different altitudes. Think of the CRO as the person who decides *what the revenue machine should be* and the VP of Sales as the person who *runs one of its most important gears*. Below, we break down scope, cost signals, org-chart placement, the maturity stage each one fits, and how to tell which your company actually needs right now — because hiring the wrong altitude is one of the most common and costly mistakes early-stage and lower-mid-market companies make. ## What does a fractional CRO actually own that a VP of Sales does not? A Chief Revenue Officer is accountable for *all revenue-generating functions*, not just the closing motion. That means the CRO's mandate spans marketing (demand generation and pipeline creation), sales (new logos and expansion), customer success (retention, renewals, net revenue retention), revenue operations (the systems, data, and process connecting the three), and often pricing and packaging. When any one of those functions underperforms, it lands on the CRO's desk. A fractional CRO does this same job on a part-time basis — usually for a company that needs C-level revenue strategy but cannot yet justify a full-time executive comp package. A VP of Sales, by contrast, owns the sales organization and nothing above it. Their world is quota attainment, rep productivity, pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, sales-cycle length, and win rates. They hire, ramp, coach, and hold the sales team accountable. Critically, a VP of Sales inherits the go-to-market motion rather than defining it — they are handed an ICP, a set of channels, and a pricing model, and they build a team to execute against them. If the ICP is wrong or the channels don't produce pipeline, a VP of Sales will burn quarters trying to sell harder against a broken strategy, because fixing the strategy is above their pay grade. The distinction between owning the *whole* motion and owning *execution inside* the motion is the single clearest way to tell these roles apart. For a deeper breakdown of how these functions connect, see the [revenue operations architecture guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-architecture-101). The practical test: ask "who is accountable if marketing generates plenty of leads but they never convert, *and* customers churn after six months?" If the answer is one person, that person is a CRO. A VP of Sales would legitimately say "the leads were bad and retention isn't my job" — and they'd be right. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Revenue Engine] --> B[Marketing / Demand Gen] A --> C[Sales] A --> D[Customer Success / Retention] A --> E[RevOps · Systems & Data] A --> F[Pricing & Packaging] CRO[Fractional CRO] -.owns all.-> A VP[Fractional VP of Sales] -.owns only.-> C style CRO fill:#ff8a00,stroke:#333,color:#fff style VP fill:#2b6cb0,stroke:#333,color:#fff style A fill:#1a202c,stroke:#333,color:#fff ``` ## How do the cost and time commitment compare? Because scope differs, so does price — and the gap is a useful signal in itself. Fractional executives are generally billed either as a monthly retainer or a day-rate, and the CRO commands a premium because the role requires cross-functional command that far fewer operators possess. A fractional CRO typically engages for a set number of days per month at a senior C-suite rate reflecting profit-and-loss-level accountability. A fractional VP of Sales usually engages at a lower rate, reflecting a narrower, execution-focused remit. We won't quote specific dollar figures here because fractional rates vary enormously by market, industry, company stage, and the individual's track record — anyone quoting a single "standard" number is guessing. What matters is the *relative* structure: expect a CRO engagement to cost meaningfully more per day than a VP of Sales engagement, and expect the CRO to spend a portion of their time in the boardroom and cross-functional leadership meetings rather than in deal reviews. If you're budgeting, the honest move is to get quotes from two or three operators for the *specific* scope you need, then compare. Whatever the numbers, the ratio holds: broader mandate, higher rate. There's also a duration difference. A fractional VP of Sales is often brought in for a defined build-or-fix window — stand up the sales team, install a repeatable process, hit a number, then hand off to a full-time hire. A fractional CRO engagement tends to be more open-ended and strategic, sometimes evolving into an ongoing advisory relationship even after full-time leaders are hired underneath them. Neither is inherently better; they solve different problems on different clocks. The [fractional leadership cost framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-exec-costs) walks through how to model these engagements against the alternative of a full-time hire plus equity. ## Where do they sit on the org chart, and who reports to whom? Org placement is where the difference becomes concrete. A CRO — fractional or full-time — reports to the CEO and sits on the executive leadership team. Reporting *up into* the CRO you'll typically find the VP of Sales, the VP of Marketing (or CMO in larger orgs), the VP or Head of Customer Success, and the Head of RevOps. In other words, **a VP of Sales frequently reports to a CRO.** That single fact resolves most of the confusion: these aren't competing titles, they're stacked layers. The CRO is one rung up. In a smaller company that has a fractional CRO but no VP of Sales yet, the CRO may temporarily perform some VP-of-Sales duties — running the pipeline review, coaching a couple of reps — but that's a stopgap, not the job. Their real value is architecting the revenue system and, often, hiring the VP of Sales who will own execution long-term. Conversely, a company with a fractional VP of Sales and no CRO has made a deliberate bet: leadership (usually the CEO or founder) is confident the go-to-market *strategy* is sound and simply needs a professional to build and run the closing engine. That bet is correct surprisingly often for founder-led companies where the founder *is* the de facto CRO and just needs sales execution offloaded. ```mermaid flowchart TD CEO[CEO / Founder] --> CRO[CRO
revenue strategy · full funnel] CRO --> VPS[VP of Sales
quota · team · pipeline] CRO --> VPM[VP of Marketing
demand gen] CRO --> VPCS[VP of Customer Success
retention · NRR] CRO --> RO[Head of RevOps
systems · data] VPS --> REPS[AEs · SDRs · Sales Managers] style CEO fill:#1a202c,stroke:#333,color:#fff style CRO fill:#ff8a00,stroke:#333,color:#fff style VPS fill:#2b6cb0,stroke:#333,color:#fff ``` Understanding this hierarchy also tells you the *sequencing* of hires. Most companies hire a VP of Sales before they hire a CRO, because they need execution before they need cross-functional orchestration. You bring in a CRO when you have multiple revenue functions that have grown large enough to conflict with each other — when marketing and sales are fighting over lead quality, when success is churning customers sales oversold, when nobody owns the full number. That's a coordination problem, and coordination across functions is the CRO's core job. ## Which one does my company actually need right now? Match the hire to the *problem*, not to the prestige of the title. Here's a diagnostic framework that cuts through most cases. **Hire a fractional VP of Sales when:** your go-to-market motion works but your sales execution doesn't. Symptoms include reps missing quota with no consistent playbook, no reliable forecast, long or unpredictable sales cycles, a founder still closing every deal personally, or a sales team that grew fast and now lacks a manager who can coach and hold the line. You know your ICP, your pricing converts when the right person sells it, and marketing produces enough pipeline. You need someone to build the machine that turns pipeline into closed revenue reliably and repeatably. This is a *depth* problem inside one function. **Hire a fractional CRO when:** the problem spans functions or nobody owns the whole number. Symptoms include marketing and sales blaming each other, healthy top-of-funnel that never converts to revenue, strong new-logo sales undermined by high churn, no coherent story connecting pricing to positioning to retention, or a board asking for a revenue strategy nobody on the team can articulate end-to-end. You don't just need better closing — you need someone to design how the entire revenue engine fits together and hold every part accountable to one integrated plan. This is a *breadth* and *architecture* problem. A useful gut-check: **if you can name the exact number you want hit and you already know how you'd hit it, you need a VP of Sales. If you're not even sure which lever is broken — acquisition, conversion, expansion, or retention — you need a CRO to diagnose the whole system first.** Many companies waste a year hiring a VP of Sales to fix what is actually a strategy problem, then wonder why a great sales leader couldn't move the number. Our [go-to-market diagnostic](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/gtm-diagnostic-framework) helps founders pinpoint which lever is actually broken before they commit to a hire. One more consideration: company stage. Seed and early-Series-A companies with a single motion and a founder-seller almost always want a VP of Sales first. Series B and beyond, with multiple channels and functions that have started to collide, are where a CRO earns their premium. Fractional versions of both exist precisely because these needs often arise *before* a company can afford — or justify — the full-time version of either role. ## What skills and background distinguish the two operators? The people who fill these roles come from different career paths, and knowing the profile helps you vet candidates. A strong fractional VP of Sales is a career sales leader: they've carried a bag, run a team, built a sales process, and lived inside a CRM. Their superpowers are coaching, pipeline management, forecasting discipline, hiring closers, and installing a repeatable methodology (MEDDIC, Challenger, Command of the Message, whatever fits). You want deep, specific expertise in *selling your kind of product to your kind of buyer.* A fractional VP of Sales who's only ever sold six-figure enterprise deals may struggle to build a high-velocity, self-serve motion, and vice versa. Motion-fit matters more than raw seniority. A strong fractional CRO has a broader résumé that spans more than one revenue function — often someone who's led sales *and* marketing, or run RevOps, or owned a full P&L. Their superpower is orchestration: aligning incentives across teams, connecting pricing to positioning to retention, building a data and operations backbone so the functions actually talk to each other, and communicating a revenue strategy to a board. A CRO who's only ever run sales and never touched marketing or success is really a VP of Sales with a fancier title — a red flag worth probing in interviews. Ask a CRO candidate how they'd fix a churn problem or restructure pricing; if they only talk about the sales team, they're mis-titled. The [RevOps talent evaluation checklist](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-hiring-signals) covers the interview questions that separate true cross-functional CROs from re-titled sales leaders. Both roles, in their fractional form, share one non-obvious skill the full-time versions need less of: the ability to embed fast, diagnose quickly, and transfer knowledge to permanent staff. A fractional executive is often building the thing they'll eventually hand off, so "makes themselves replaceable" is a feature, not a bug. The best fractional operators leave behind a documented system and a hired successor, not a dependency. ## Related questions ### Can one person be both a fractional CRO and VP of Sales? Yes, in small companies a single fractional operator often wears both hats — architecting revenue strategy while also running the sales team directly — because there isn't yet enough scale to justify separating the roles. It's common but temporary; the roles split as the company grows. ### Does a fractional CRO replace the need for a CMO? Not usually. A CRO orchestrates marketing as part of the revenue engine but rarely does hands-on brand, product marketing, or creative work. In larger orgs the CMO owns marketing execution and reports into (or partners alongside) the CRO. In smaller ones, a CRO may cover demand gen strategy without replacing a full marketing leader. ### Is a fractional VP of Sales the same as a sales consultant? No. A consultant advises and hands you a deck; a fractional VP of Sales embeds in the org, carries accountability for the number, manages the team directly, and owns outcomes. The distinction is ownership — a fractional VP is on the hook for results, not just recommendations. ### When should you convert a fractional role to full-time? Convert when the workload consistently exceeds the fractional days available and the strategic foundation is stable enough to warrant a permanent, dedicated owner — typically once the function is producing predictable results and the main job shifts from *building* to *running and scaling.* ### Which role should a Series A startup hire first? Almost always a VP of Sales. At Series A most companies have one motion and need execution muscle to make it repeatable, not full-funnel orchestration. The CRO hire makes sense later, once multiple revenue functions exist and start to conflict. ## FAQ **What does "fractional" actually mean in these titles?** Fractional means part-time and embedded — the executive works a set number of days per week or month for your company while typically serving a few other clients, giving you senior leadership at a fraction of full-time cost and commitment. They're genuine members of your team during their engaged time, not outside advisors. **Does a VP of Sales report to a CRO?** Typically yes. In organizations that have both, the VP of Sales owns the sales function and reports up to the CRO, who owns all revenue functions including sales, marketing, and customer success. They are stacked layers, not competing peers. **Is a CRO more senior than a VP of Sales?** Yes. The CRO is a C-suite executive reporting to the CEO with accountability for the entire revenue P&L, while the VP of Sales is a functional leader responsible for the sales team specifically. The CRO sits one rung higher on the org chart. **Can a company have a CRO but no VP of Sales?** Yes, especially smaller companies where the CRO temporarily runs the sales team directly until the company grows enough to justify a dedicated VP of Sales underneath them. It's a common stage in a company's scaling journey. **Which role is cheaper to hire fractionally?** A fractional VP of Sales generally costs less than a fractional CRO because the mandate is narrower — sales execution versus full-funnel revenue architecture. Exact rates vary widely by market, stage, and individual track record, so get scoped quotes rather than relying on a single benchmark. **Do these roles work for non-SaaS or non-tech companies?** Yes. While the titles originated in tech and SaaS, fractional CROs and VPs of Sales increasingly serve manufacturing, professional services, healthcare, and other B2B sectors where the same distinction applies: full revenue engine ownership versus sales-function execution. **How long does a typical fractional engagement last?** It varies. A fractional VP of Sales often engages for a defined build-and-hand-off window of several months to a year or more, while a fractional CRO engagement tends to run longer and more open-ended given its strategic nature. Both should have clear success criteria and an exit or conversion plan. **What's the fastest way to tell which one I need?** Ask whether your problem lives inside sales execution or spans multiple revenue functions. If reps just need better management and a repeatable process, hire a VP of Sales. If marketing, sales, and retention are misaligned and no one owns the whole number, hire a CRO. ## Sources - [Harvard Business Review — The Chief Revenue Officer's Mandate](https://hbr.org/) - [Gartner — Revenue Operations and Go-to-Market Alignment Research](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales) - [SaaStr — When to Hire a VP of Sales vs. a CRO](https://www.saastr.com/) - [Pavilion — Revenue Leadership Benchmarks and Role Definitions](https://www.joinpavilion.com/) - [Bessemer Venture Partners — Scaling the Revenue Org](https://www.bvp.com/atlas) - [First Round Review — Building Your First Sales Team](https://review.firstround.com/) - [RevGenius — Fractional Leadership in RevOps](https://www.revgenius.com/) - [OpenView Partners — SaaS Go-to-Market Benchmarks](https://openviewpartners.com/) ## Related on PULSE - [RevOps Architecture 101: How the Full Revenue Engine Fits Together](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-architecture-101) - [Fractional Executive Cost Framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-exec-costs) - [Go-to-Market Diagnostic Framework](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/gtm-diagnostic-framework) - [RevOps Hiring Signals: Vetting Senior Revenue Leaders](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-hiring-signals)
